title: The Slowest Race
summary: Pace a champion racing snail with a free electron in a copper wire: set the current, the wire and the voltage for a dead heat.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 3.5, Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
concepts: Current as charge per second, I = Q/t
The drift is slow, the signal is fast
learningOutcome: The student can find a current from a count of electrons and give its direction, use I = nAev_d and v_d = μE, and explain why a lamp lights at once while electrons crawl.

levels.title: Start gate
levels.adds: Baseline: current is charge per second, I = Ne/t, and the conventional current points the opposite way to the electrons’ drift (Section 3.2).
hints: The charge through the gate is the number of electrons times 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Current is that charge divided by the time in seconds.
Electrons are negative, so the current arrow points the other way to their drift.

levels.title: A slow crawl
levels.adds: New idea: I = nAev_d, so to keep pace with a snail the current must be n e A times its speed (Ex 3.9, Example 3.1).
hints: First find Shelly’s pace: the track length divided by her record time, in mm per second.
I = n e A v_d. With A in mm² and v_d in mm/s, n e A v_d comes to 13.6 × A × v_d amperes.
Check the units: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m² and 1 mm/s = 10⁻³ m/s.

levels.title: Thick and thin
levels.adds: New idea: at a fixed current v_d ∝ 1/A, so a thinner wire drifts faster, and the field that starts the drift moves at 3 × 10⁸ m/s (Example 3.2).
hints: The finish lamp lit when the field reached it at 3 × 10⁸ m/s: each nanosecond is 30 cm of wire.
Shelly’s pace is that length divided by her record time.
A = I ÷ (n e v_d): the same current drifts faster in a thinner wire.

levels.title: Mobility
levels.adds: More steps: v_d = μE with E = V/L sets the pace, then I = nAev_d sets the lamp’s current through the wire’s area (Section 3.5.1).
hints: The field in the wire is the voltage across it divided by its length.
v_d = μE, so V = v_d × L ÷ μ. Mind the 10⁻³ in μ and the millivolts on the dial.
Then pick the area that makes n e A v_d equal the lamp’s current.

misconceptions: Electrons race along a wire at nearly the speed of light
A lamp lights at once because electrons travel instantly from the switch
Conventional current flows the same way as the electrons
A thinner wire has a slower drift speed
